design_detail: Cross-sectional, non-randomized comparison of people trained and not trained by six US overdose-training and naloxone-distribution programmes (Chicago; State of New Mexico; San Francisco; Baltimore; New York City: Citiwide Harm Reduction and Positive Health Project), October 2005 to July 2006. Programme staff recruited five trained and five untrained participants per site (actually 30 and 32), who completed a self-administered questionnaire rating 16 written scenarios, drawn from overdose experiences reported by people who inject drugs, as opioid overdose, non-opioid overdose, not an overdose, or not enough information, and saying whether naloxone was indicated. The answer key came from 11 medical experts combined by latent class analysis: 9 scenarios were opioid overdoses requiring naloxone and 7 were non-opioid overdoses or not overdoses, not requiring it. Scores were compared by t-tests and exploratory regression, and agreement with the experts by kappa (PDF pp. 2–5, Methods). Appraised with ROBINS-I because training is an intervention compared between non-randomized groups.
can_establish: That, in these six programmes in 2005–2006, people the programmes had trained scored higher than people they had not trained on recognising opioid overdose in written scenarios and on deciding when naloxone was indicated, and that both groups often misjudged scenarios that were non-opioid overdoses or not overdoses.
cannot_establish: That training caused the higher scores (no randomization and no pre-training scores; participants chosen by programme staff), how people perform at a real overdose, which signs of overdose were recognised or missed (no scenario-level results are reported), or any effect on deaths or costs.

sample.recruitment: Staff of programmes approached at a national conference on opioid overdose recruited participants at programme sites where people who use or used drugs gather (for example needle exchanges and drop-in sites); participants were paid $10 (PDF p. 4, Methods › Study procedure).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Trained participants had been trained by the recruiting programme, a median of 8 months before (range 1–80 months) (PDF p. 5, Results, 1st paragraph). Three untrained participants reported training elsewhere (in a CPR course, at a long-term treatment facility, in Vancouver) and were counted as untrained because that training was not aimed at overdose response or was more than 9 years earlier (Table 2 footnote, PDF p. 5).
sample.demographics: 72.6% male; 85.5% currently or formerly used drugs; 14 (22.6%) syringe-exchange staff; needle-exchange employees were 30.0% of the trained and 15.6% of the untrained group (Table 2, PDF p. 5). No data on age, race, ethnicity or drugs used, to preserve anonymity and limit burden (PDF p. 4, Evaluation tool, 2nd paragraph).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single questionnaire). Some item-level data are missing without explanation: degrees of freedom of 59 and 58 in some tests, and 962 rather than 992 ratings (62 × 16; editors' calculation).
sample.selection_effects: Non-random recruitment by programme staff, who might choose engaged or knowledgeable people; the authors say they asked for random samples and think biased selection was unlikely given staff time constraints (PDF p. 9, Discussion, 7th paragraph). Untrained participants were recruited at the same harm-reduction sites, so both groups were in contact with these programmes; trained participants were more often needle-exchange staff.

exposure.measurement: Training status as recorded by the recruiting programme and the questionnaire's training-history item (Table 2). The programmes' trainings were brief (about 15 to 120 minutes), mixed didactic and interactive parts, and all covered recognising and responding to opioid overdose and calling 911; all six explicitly taught telling an opioid overdose from a 'heavy nod'; two (San Francisco, Baltimore) explicitly covered non-opioid (for example stimulant) overdose and two partly; four tested knowledge after training (PDF p. 2, Methods › Summary of training programs; Table 1, PDF p. 3).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable (training). Time since training: median 8 months, range 1–80 months.
exposure.polysubstance: Drug use was not recorded (PDF p. 4).

comparison.controls: 32 people not trained by the recruiting programme, recruited at the same sites; and the consensus of 11 medical experts, which served as the answer key.
comparison.matching: Recruitment was balanced by site (five trained and five untrained requested). The groups were similar in sex, background, overdose history, witnessing and responding (Table 2), with no adjustment beyond exploratory regression; age, race, ethnicity and drug use were not measured.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-training scores. Prior knowledge, motivation, literacy, age, drug use and earlier experience with naloxone were not measured or only partly measured.

outcomes.instruments: Questionnaire with 16 written scenarios, scored 0–16 for overdose recognition and 0–16 for naloxone indication against the experts' key; self-rated expertise (1 low to 5 high) in identifying opioid overdose, when to use naloxone and non-opioid overdose; history of witnessing and responding to overdoses (PDF p. 4, Methods › Evaluation tool). Development and validation are reported elsewhere (ref. 20, a 2006 conference abstract); the scenarios were selected from 60 experiences reported in a study of public injecting (ref. 21).
outcomes.validity_norms: The answer key is the experts' latent-class consensus; the instrument's validity is cited from a conference abstract; the scenario texts are not printed.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Missed opportunity' = an opioid-overdose scenario for which naloxone was not indicated by the respondent; 'wasted resources' = naloxone indicated for a non-opioid overdose or non-overdose scenario (PDF p. 6). The 7-item category merges non-opioid overdoses and situations that were not overdoses.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: nine knowledge and self-rating comparisons (Table 3), four exploratory regressions (Table 4), and further chi-square, rank and kappa analyses, without correction.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Self-administered questionnaire scored against a fixed key; site staff, who knew participants' training status, were available to answer questions or to administer the questionnaire to people with literacy problems (PDF p. 4).

analysis.effect_sizes: Table 3 (PDF p. 6), trained vs untrained, mean (SD): opioid overdose recognised 7.13 (1.38) vs 5.18 (2.55) of 9, t60 = −3.76, P < 0.001; non-opioid or no overdose recognised 4.63 (1.40) vs 4.28 (1.94) of 7, t60 = −0.81, P = 0.42; recognition total 11.77 (1.92) vs 9.47 (3.48) of 16, t48.93 = −3.24, P < 0.005; naloxone correctly indicated 6.93 (1.76) vs 5.77 (2.30) of 9, t59 = −2.20, P < 0.05; naloxone correctly not indicated 6.60 (0.72) vs 5.32 (1.94) of 7, t38.32 = −3.43, P < 0.001; naloxone total 13.53 (1.96) vs 11.09 (2.32) of 16, t59 = −4.38, P < 0.0001. The authors report Cohen's d of 0.97 for overdose knowledge and 1.1 for naloxone indication knowledge (PDF p. 9). Editors' calculation (pooled SD, approximate 95% CI): d = 0.94 (0.42 to 1.47) for opioid-overdose recognition, 0.81 (0.29 to 1.33) for the recognition total, 0.57 (0.05 to 1.08) for naloxone in opioid scenarios and 1.13 (0.59 to 1.68) for the naloxone total. Agreement with experts (PDF p. 8): weighted kappa 0.85 (0.72–0.98) for trained and 0.48 (0.18–0.77) for untrained respondents; trained vs untrained 0.56 (0.22–0.89); for naloxone, kappa 1.0 between experts and trained respondents and 0.75 (0.44–1.0) for untrained respondents. Regressions (Table 4, PDF p. 7): standardized β for training 0.41 (opioid recognition), 0.51 (naloxone) and 0.47 (overall, with self-rated opioid expertise β 0.24); ever responding to an overdose, adjusted OR 2.06 (1.05–4.03) for self-rated opioid-overdose expertise and 2.6 (1.31–5.21) for non-opioid expertise.
analysis.covariates: Exploratory regressions entered only variables with significant bivariate associations (four or fewer), chosen by non-automated backward and stepwise selection (PDF p. 5, Data analysis).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Approved by the Human Investigations Committee of Yale University School of Medicine (PDF p. 5); no protocol or registration mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Scenario-level results (which situations or signs were misjudged) are not reported and the scenarios are not printed; site-level results appear only as no significant differences (PDF p. 6).
analysis.power: The authors report power above 0.8 to detect at least one independent regression variable, and insufficient power for site-specific differences (PDF pp. 5, 9).

interpretation_gap.results_show: People trained by six US programmes got more written opioid-overdose scenarios right than untrained people (about 7.1 vs 5.2 of 9) and decided correctly about naloxone more often (13.5 vs 11.1 of 16). On average, trained respondents still did not choose naloxone in about 2 of the 9 opioid-overdose scenarios (untrained about 3), and both groups did similarly poorly on scenarios that were non-opioid overdoses or not overdoses (4.6 vs 4.3 of 7). The comparison is a single cross-sectional one between non-randomized groups recruited by programme staff.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that training programmes improve participants' ability to recognise and respond to opioid overdoses, and that trained, confident people who use drugs may effectively prevent overdose mortality (PDF p. 1); the Discussion says training improved recognition significantly (PDF p. 8) and that the study provides key evidence that the programmes are effective and probably cost-effective (PDF p. 9, Discussion, 6th paragraph). These causal and cost claims rest on a one-time comparison of 30 and 32 non-randomly recruited people, with no baseline, no observed real overdoses, no mortality data and no costs. The abstract's statement that trained respondents were as skilled as medical experts (weighted kappa 0.85; kappa 1.0 for naloxone) cannot describe individuals, since trained individuals averaged 84.6% correct on naloxone; the unit of the kappa analysis is not stated, and two of the eleven experts are also named among staff of the evaluation sites (PDF p. 9). The Discussion reads the 7-item scores as low non-opioid overdose knowledge (PDF p. 8), but that category merges non-opioid overdoses with situations that were not overdoses.

timeline.event: Seal et al. (2005), naloxone distribution and CPR training pilot for people who inject drugs in San Francisco, cited among programmes claiming falls in overdose deaths (ref. 14). Not read.

Green, Grau and Heimer (2006), conference abstract on medical experts' agreement about overdose symptoms reported by people who use drugs, cited for the development and validation of the 16-scenario tool (ref. 20). Not read.

Walley et al. (2013): Massachusetts communities with more enrolment in overdose education and nasal naloxone distribution had lower opioid-overdose death rates (adjusted rate ratios 0.73 and 0.54 by enrolment level) in an ecological analysis (card sc_walley_2013).
McDonald and Strang (2016), systematic review of take-home naloxone programmes: 22 observational studies, none randomized (card sc_mcdonald_2016).

replication.where_it_stands: No replication of this scenario-recognition comparison was read for this card. Evidence that naloxone programmes reduce deaths comes from observational and ecological studies (Walley et al., 2013; review by McDonald and Strang, 2016), not from this knowledge study. Which overdose signs people miss, and how well they tell a heavy nod from an overdose in real situations, is not answered by this paper.

funding.funder: The evaluation was conducted with support from an institutional training grant for T. C. G.: NIMH 5T32MH020031 (PDF p. 9, Acknowledgements).
funding.declared_conflicts: No declaration of interests in the version read.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the Department of Epidemiology and Public Health, Yale University School of Medicine, and the Yale Center for Interdisciplinary Research on AIDS (PDF p. 1). Two of the 11 medical experts whose consensus set the answer key (Sharon Stancliff and Bernie Lieving) are also named among staff of evaluation sites (Harm Reduction Coalition, Positive Health Project, New York; New Mexico Department of Health) (PDF p. 9). A flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized or stepped-wedge trial of overdose-response training among people who use opioids, measuring recognition before training, after it and at follow-up with validated, published scenarios (reporting which signs are missed, including a heavy nod against an overdose), and recording real overdose responses and outcomes, with the answer key set by experts independent of the programmes.

domains.note: Trained and untrained people may differ in motivation, engagement, prior knowledge, literacy, age and drug use, none measured; needle-exchange staff were more common among the trained (30.0% vs 15.6%); no baseline; regressions exploratory with few covariates.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Programme staff chose participants; the trained people available to them may be the most engaged; numbers recruited and refusals are not reported.
Training status defined by the recruiting programme; three people trained elsewhere counted as untrained; time since training 1–80 months.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Training differed by site in length (about 15–120 minutes), format and content (non-opioid overdose covered explicitly at two sites), so 'trained' covers different interventions.
Item-level missing data implied (degrees of freedom of 59 and 58; 962 of 992 ratings) and not explained.

Written hypothetical scenarios rather than real overdoses; validity cited from a conference abstract; scenarios not printed; staff who knew training status could help with completion; the answer key was partly set by experts who are also staff of evaluated programmes.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: No protocol; scenario-level and site-level results not reported; stepwise exploratory models; the recognition percentages and one P value do not match their own numbers.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The knowledge differences are large and consistent across outcomes, but attributing them to training is at serious risk of bias from confounding and staff selection of participants, and the outcome is performance on written scenarios scored against a key partly set by programme staff. Citable for: in 2005–2006, people trained by six US programmes scored higher than untrained people on written opioid-overdose scenarios and naloxone decisions; both groups often misjudged non-opioid or non-overdose scenarios; on average even trained respondents did not choose naloxone in about 2 of 9 opioid-overdose scenarios; all six programmes taught telling a heavy nod from an overdose. Not citable for: training causing better recognition, performance at real overdoses, which signs people recognise, effects on mortality or cost-effectiveness, or trained laypeople individually matching medical experts.

key_findings.finding: 62 respondents (30 trained, 32 untrained) took part between October 2005 and July 2006 at six programmes; 72.6% were male, 85.5% currently or formerly used drugs and 22.6% were syringe-exchange staff; trained respondents had been trained a median of 8 months earlier (range 1–80 months).

Overdose experience: 45.8% had overdosed (n = 27; median three overdoses, IQR 4), 72% had witnessed an overdose (n = 44; median 7.5 witnessed, IQR 11) and 62.3% had responded to one (n = 38; 86.4% of those who had witnessed one); trained and untrained respondents did not differ significantly in demographics or overdose experience.

Trained respondents recognised more of the nine opioid-overdose scenarios (mean 7.13 vs 5.18, t60 = −3.76, P < 0.001) but not more of the seven non-opioid or non-overdose scenarios (4.63 vs 4.28, t60 = −0.81, P = 0.42); recognition totals were 11.77 vs 9.47 of 16 (t48.93 = −3.24, P < 0.005).
key_findings.locator: Results › Overdose and naloxone knowledge; Table 3
key_findings.note: Table 3 and the text give 85.2% vs 68.3% correct for recognition, which do not match 11.77 and 9.47 of 16 (73.6% and 59.2%, editors' calculation); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Naloxone decisions: trained respondents missed fewer opioid-overdose scenarios needing naloxone (2.1 vs 3.2 of 9; correct 6.93 vs 5.77, t59 = −2.20, P < 0.05) and recommended naloxone less often where it was not indicated (0.4 vs 1.7 of 7; t38.32 = −3.43, P < 0.001); naloxone totals were 13.53 vs 11.09 of 16 (84.6% vs 69.3%; t59 = −4.38, P < 0.0001).
key_findings.locator: Results › Naloxone response: 'missed opportunities', 'wasted resources'; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Self-rated expertise was higher among trained respondents for identifying opioid overdose (3.77 vs 3.22 on a 1–5 scale, t60 = 2.14, P < 0.05) and when to use naloxone (3.83 vs 2.63, t60 = 5.03, P < 0.0001), but not for non-opioid overdose (3.39 vs 3.22, t58 = 0.59, P = 0.56).
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (continued on PDF p. 6); Table 3 (PDF p. 6)

key_findings.finding: In exploratory regressions, training was the only independent predictor of opioid-overdose recognition (standardized β 0.41, P < 0.001) and of naloxone knowledge (β 0.51, P < 0.001); overall knowledge was predicted by training (β 0.47) and self-rated opioid-overdose expertise (β 0.24, P < 0.05). Ever having responded to an overdose was associated with self-rated expertise in recognising opioid overdose (adjusted OR 2.06, 95% CI 1.05–4.03) and non-opioid overdose (adjusted OR 2.6, 1.31–5.21).
key_findings.locator: Results › Multivariable analyses (PDF p. 6); Table 4 (PDF p. 7)

key_findings.finding: Of 962 ratings, 43.9% (n = 422) were opioid overdose, 39% (n = 375) not an overdose or non-opioid overdose and 17.2% (n = 165) unsure. The experts used the unsure category for 25.6% of their codes against 16.0% for trained respondents. Weighted kappa with the experts was 0.85 (95% CI 0.72–0.98) for trained and 0.48 (0.18–0.77) for untrained respondents (trained vs untrained 0.56, 0.22–0.89); for naloxone, kappa was 1.0 between experts and trained respondents and 0.75 (0.44–1.0) for untrained respondents.
key_findings.locator: Results › Comparison of participants to medical experts, 1st paragraph (begins PDF p. 7) and 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 8)
key_findings.note: The unit of the kappa analysis (individual ratings or each group's pooled answer per scenario) is not stated; a kappa of 1.0 cannot reflect individuals, given trained individuals' 84.6% naloxone accuracy.

key_findings.finding: Untrained respondents more often reported never having responded to an overdose (48.4% vs 27.6%, χ²3 = 8.62, P < 0.05); trained respondents more often had responded within the past year (37.9% vs 25.8%) or 1–5 years earlier (31.0% vs 9.7%; linear trend χ²1 = 3.94, P < 0.05). More recent witnessing of an overdose was only marginally associated with training (OR 2.71, 95% CI 0.95–7.71).
key_findings.locator: Results › Responses to overdose situations and time since training; Witnessing and responding to overdose; Figure 2

key_findings.finding: All six programmes explicitly taught how to tell an opioid overdose from a 'heavy nod'; two (San Francisco, Baltimore) explicitly covered non-opioid (for example stimulant) overdose, two partly; four required some knowledge test after training; trainings lasted about 15 to 120 minutes, in settings from needle exchanges to street corners and homes.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Summary of training programs, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (PDF p. 2); Table 1 (PDF p. 3)

key_findings.finding: The 16 scenarios were selected from 60 overdose experiences reported by people who inject drugs in a study of public injecting; 11 medical experts classified each, and latent class analysis of their answers gave the key: 9 opioid overdoses, all requiring naloxone, and 7 non-opioid overdoses or non-overdoses, not requiring it. The scenario texts are not printed and results are not given by scenario.

Limitations stated by the authors: small sample with insufficient power for site differences; observational design open to self-report and reporting bias; non-random recruitment at each site; witnessed and responded-to overdoses not necessarily the same events; limited demographic data, so residual confounding is possible.

reporting_issues.issue: The average percentages correct for overdose recognition (85.2% trained, 68.3% untrained; Table 3 and text) do not match the 16-item means (11.77 and 9.47, i.e. 73.6% and 59.2%, editors' calculation); the text even pairs 85.2% with '11.7 versus 9.5 of 16 correct'. The naloxone percentages (84.6%, 69.3%) do match their means.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite recognition as 11.8 vs 9.5 of 16 scenarios, not as 85.2% vs 68.3%.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract describes ten participants recruited from each of six sites, but n = 62, with 11 at Chicago and at Citiwide (Table 2).

The expert comparison analyses 962 raw ratings, whereas 62 respondents rating 16 scenarios give 992 (editors' calculation); together with degrees of freedom of 59 and 58 in some tests, this implies unexplained missing answers.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the amount and pattern of missing answers are unknown.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 4 prints P < 0.001 for the adjusted OR of 2.6 (95% CI 1.31–5.21); that interval corresponds to P of about 0.007 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the association remains nominally significant but is weaker than printed.

reporting_issues.issue: The unit of the kappa analysis is not stated. A kappa of 1.0 between experts and trained respondents for naloxone cannot be agreement of individual respondents, since trained individuals averaged 13.53 of 16 correct (84.6%) and missed naloxone in about 2.1 of 9 opioid-overdose scenarios; it presumably compares the trained group's pooled answers with the experts' key.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's statement that trained respondents were as skilled as medical experts should not be cited as individual equivalence.

reporting_issues.issue: Two of the 11 medical experts whose consensus set the answer key (Stancliff, Lieving) are also named among staff of the evaluation sites (Acknowledgements).
reporting_issues.consequence: Agreement between trained respondents and the key may be inflated if the same people shaped both the curricula and the key.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 2 text gives 48.4% of untrained respondents as never having responded to an overdose, while Table 2 gives 17 of 32 untrained respondents (53.1%) as having responded, which implies 46.9%; the denominators differ (31 vs 32) without explanation.
